articles.title: New reasons not to be depressed about depression
articles.summary: President Trump’s administration directed $50 million in federal funding toward accelerating research into psychedelic treatments like psilocybin to help combat the rising number of U.S. adults suffering from treatment-resistant depression.
articles.body:
The number of adults being treated for depression has grown significantly over the last 10 years. And many patients have struggled to find an effective therapy that helps them manage the disease.

Fortunately, medical researchers are trying to address that problem. And President Trump’s effort to ramp up research into psychedelic treatments could provide a much-needed boost.

A recent Gallup poll reports the number of U.S. adults with depression is up about 8 percentage points since 2015, to an estimated 48 million Americans. The Yale School of Medicine says that nearly one-fifth of U.S. adults will be diagnosed with major depressive disorder at some point in their lives.

Every year, depression forces millions of Americans out of the workforce, wreaks havoc on their family lives, and inflicts immense damage on the economy. Yale Medicine reports depression and other mental illnesses cost U.S. workers an estimated $333 billion in 2019 .

Depression is notoriously difficult to treat. Unlike medicines such as antibiotics and pain relievers that tend to work for the vast majority of people, many with mental illness never find a medication, or multiple medications, that work well for them. An analysis in the journal Nature found that nearly half of all patients with major depressive disorder don’t respond to at least two available antidepressants, which qualifies as “treatment-resistant depression.”

That challenge can have disastrous consequences at work and at home. A parent struggling with severe depression may find it difficult to maintain the routines children depend on, from helping with schoolwork to preparing meals. Families also face mounting financial strains due to missed workdays, increased childcare expenses, and years of ongoing medical costs tied to unsuccessful treatment attempts.

For people with persistent depression, symptoms like exhaustion, disrupted sleep, impaired concentration, and emotional distress can make it difficult to perform consistently at work or force them to take repeated or extended medical leave. As a result of multiple medical appointments, medication changes, hospitalizations, and ongoing treatment, they may incur more than twice the annual health care costs of patients without depression.

Sadly, people with the most persistent forms of depression currently have only two Food and Drug Administration-approved treatments available.

Americans facing this disease deserve the opportunity to try every scientifically supported treatment option through safe, regulated means.

The good news is physicians and medical researchers are investigating new options, and there is evidence that psychedelic substances like psilocybin could provide an effective therapy for many with treatment-resistant depression. For example, Dr. Benjamin Kelmendi, a psychiatrist at Yale, and his colleagues have initiated several clinical studies investigating how psilocybin alters the brain, leading to improved symptoms of depression.

Clinical studies are critical. The placebo effect — a perceived change in a person’s physical or mental health resulting from their belief that they are receiving medical treatment — is especially prevalent in studies on depression. Researchers need to determine if the new drugs actually work, what their proper formulation should be, and if they are safe and effective. They’re doing that now.

A Johns Hopkins randomized trial found that 71 percent of participants with treatment-resistant depression who received psilocybin experienced a clinically significant reduction in symptoms with minimal side effects and a low potential for addiction.

Ketamine and MDMA treatments have similarly helped patients who repeatedly sought — and failed to find — relief from more traditional antidepressants.

These findings warrant serious study in regulated medical settings. Some people use psychedelics and other mind-altering drugs for recreational purposes and to self-medicate, often based on anecdotal claims by non-professionals touting a substance’s curative powers. That is dangerous and should be avoided. Those with symptoms of depression or other mental conditions should see a doctor.

Clinical trials are already occurring across the country, and it’s possible that the Food and Drug Administration will soon approve new treatments to be used under professional medical care. President Trump’s recent executive order directs $50 million in federal funding to advance psychedelic treatments for mental illness, helping accelerate research and evaluation of these medicines.

The status quo is failing too many patients. In 2024, suicide claimed nearly 49,000 lives , and one estimate says that two-thirds of them were depression related. And even when depression doesn’t lead to an irreversible loss, it drains patients and their families emotionally and financially.

People living with debilitating conditions deserve every reasonable chance to find relief. It’s up to policymakers to explore every avenue, including researching and reviewing psychedelic treatments, to make that possible.

Merrill Matthews is the Texas state chair of Our Republican Legacy.

articles.title: Duffy thanks Zeldin for getting rid of ‘stop-start’ feature in cars: ‘I hate it’
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Monday commended Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin for targeting his “pet peeve” — an auto feature intended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. “You know the on-off, the stop-start button on your car? I hate that thing,” Duffy told the crowd at an event in Detroit. “Thank you, Lee…
articles.body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Monday commended Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Administrator Lee Zeldin for targeting his “pet peeve” — an auto feature intended to reduce greenhouse gas emissions.

“You know the on-off, the stop-start button on your car? I hate that thing,” Duffy told the crowd at an event in Detroit. “Thank you, Lee Zeldin. He’s gotten rid of it, and the first cars without the start-stop button are rolling off the line.”

In February, the EPA announced it would axe federal incentives for vehicle manufacturers that include the feature in their models. Former President Obama’s administration introduced “off-cycle” credits for vehicles that used the technology in 2012 as a way to reduce greenhouse gases.

The tech automatically stops an engine when the car is not moving and starts again when the driver presses the pedal. It cut nearly 10 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions annually as of 2023, according to Battery Council International .

In a statement announcing the change, Zeldin pushed back against the fuel efficiency regulations.

“Not only do many people find start-stop annoying, but it kills the battery of your car without any significant benefit to the environment,” he said. “The Trump EPA is proudly fixing this stupid feature at Trump speed.”

The elimination of the start-stop button credits was part of the Trump administration’s broader efforts to reverse federal emission rules to reduce costs for manufacturers and consumers.

Earlier this year, the EPA also rescinded a 2009 endangerment finding under the Obama administration that held greenhouse gas emissions from vehicles pose a threat to public health. The finding was used to require automakers to follow certain fuel efficiency standards , such as hitting an average of more than 50 miles per gallon across their fleets.

President Trump slammed these regulations as “ridiculous” during White House remarks in which he announced his administration would cancel the finding. He called the move “the single largest deregulatory action in American history.”

The president also downplayed concerns about the impact of these actions on Americans’ public health when asked by a reporter at a White House event.

“Don’t worry about it, because it has nothing to do with public health,” he said at the time. “This was all a scam, a giant scam.”

Justin Chen, the president of the American Federation of Government Employees Council 238, which represents thousands of EPA staffers, criticized the repeal as a “deep betrayal” of the agency’s mission.

“This rollback is nothing short of disastrous for the health and safety of our communities, and it also slams the brakes on the future EPA workers are helping to build,” Chen said in a statement following the announcement. “The clean energy and advanced vehicle industries are creating good-paying American jobs and positioning us to lead the world.”

He added, “Killing that progress now doesn’t just hurt innovation — it hurts workers, families, and the next generation.”

articles.title: When a return-to-office mandate is just about the boss’s narcissism
articles.summary: New research on remote work resistance argues that some leaders do not simply prefer the office because collaboration is easier there — they prefer it because the office gives them an audience, a hierarchy and a stage.
articles.body:
The fight over where people work has always sounded like a fight over productivity. It is increasingly clear that it is also a fight over power.

New research on remote work resistance argues that some leaders do not simply prefer the office because collaboration is easier there — they prefer it because the office gives them an audience, a hierarchy and a stage.

That distinction is important, because return-to-office mandates can be made to look rational in press releases even when they serve a much less flattering purpose in practice. When leaders say they want energy, culture and accountability, employees should ask whether the policy solves a business problem or feeds an executive need to be seen, obeyed and admired.

The study, by Marissa Shandell, Courtney Elliott, and Adam Grant, does not claim every office advocate is a narcissist, of course. But narcissistic leaders are more likely to resist remote work, because remote arrangements interfere with their pursuit of power and status. Across Fortune 500 CEOs and multi-wave surveys of leaders, the pattern held. Leaders higher in narcissistic personality traits showed stronger opposition to remote and hybrid work, and power motivation consistently helped explain why.

That finding, however, sharpens a debate stuck in the wrong vocabulary. Many executives describe the office as the home of office culture , and there is evidence that fully remote work can make collaboration networks more siloed. But culture is not the same thing as leader visibility. A healthy office helps employees coordinate, learn and build trust. An unhealthy office turns presence into tribute.

The difference determines whether people are gathering for work that benefits from proximity or being summoned to reassure a boss that the hierarchy still holds.

The office gives high-control leaders rich signals that remote tools dilute. They can read the room, interrupt, summon, stare, praise, punish and perform authority in real time. Video calls flatten that drama. Everyone becomes a square. Chat messages can be answered later. Cameras can be turned off. Employees gain more discretion over when and how they respond. For leaders driven by their own narcissistic personality traits, that discretion can feel less like flexibility and more like insubordination.

The case for flexibility is not a fantasy built by employees who dislike commuting. The best evidence is more nuanced — and more threatening to simplistic office mandates. In a randomized trial published in Nature, hybrid work-from-home two days a week improved job satisfaction, reduced quit rates by one-third, and did not damage performance reviews over the next two years.

That should have changed the burden of proof. Leaders who demand five days in the office now need evidence that the extra days create value beyond managerial comfort.

Workers are not asking for isolation as a lifestyle. Pew Research Center has found that many remote-capable employees prefer hybrid arrangements. Gallup reports that a majority of remote-capable employees favor a hybrid work strategy . The real employee demand is not disappearance but agency. People want enough shared time to collaborate but enough private control to avoid wasting their lives in commuting and performative attendance.

That is why rigid mandates can backfire. Research on workplace flexibility finds that companies issuing return-to-office mandates can face higher turnover, especially among senior, skilled and female employees, while taking longer to fill vacancies. Those findings do not prove remote work is always superior. Rather, they show that coercive office policies carry real human capital costs.

Fully remote work has costs too. A Science study on remote work and isolation found that remote work can increase time spent alone and worsen mental well-being, especially for people who live alone. That evidence strengthens the case for intentional hybrid design, not blanket office worship. The lesson is balance, not backlash.

The best leaders do not ask, “How do I get people back where I can watch them?” They ask, “Which work improves when we are together, and which work improves when people have focus and control?” That question turns flexible work policies from a perk into an operating system. It forces organizations to define the purpose of office days, the norms for remote days, the rituals for learning, and the metrics that actually matter.

It also exposes weak leadership. If a manager depends on physical presence to know whether people are working, the problem is not remote work — the problem is unclear goals, poor measurement or low trust. If an executive needs a crowded floor to feel important, the problem is not culture. The problem is ego. A workplace built around employee autonomy does not eliminate accountability. It makes accountability more explicit because employees are judged by outcomes rather than proximity.

Boards and executive teams should treat extreme anti-remote rhetoric as a governance signal. The leader who frames flexibility as laziness may be revealing more about control needs than employee performance. The leader who can name which meetings require presence, which mentoring moments need proximity, and which tasks require quiet focus is doing real management. The leader who simply says “culture” may be asking for applause.

The future of work should not be decided by the loudest person in the conference room. It should be designed around evidence, roles, customer needs, collaboration patterns and retention risks. Leaders who want a practical roadmap can learn from a thoughtful hybrid work model that treats flexibility as a business discipline rather than an ideological trophy.

The office still matters. So does remote work. The mistake is letting status-hungry leaders turn a management choice into a loyalty test. The healthiest organizations will stop asking employees to worship at the office altar and start asking a better question: where does the work work best?

Gleb Tsipursky, Ph.D., serves as the CEO of the future-of-work consultancy Disaster Avoidance Experts and wrote “ The Psychology of AI Adoption at Work: From Resistance to Results ” and “ ChatGPT for Leaders and Content Creators . “

articles.title: Obama-era mandate slashed after being blamed for 'skyrocketing' housing costs
articles.summary: A new Trump admin housing directive aims to tackle the U.S.'s housing affordability crunch by ending Obama-era rule allowing indefinite liability for property owners over past building design errors.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: In a bid to tackle the nation’s housing affordability crisis, the Trump administration has scrapped a controversial Obama-era mandate blamed for driving up property costs and stifling the affordable housing supply. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), alongside the Department of Justice, jointly rescinded an Obama-era policy that allowed third parties to file accessibility-related complaints over original building design flaws indefinitely, putting subsequent building owners on the hook for millions of dollars years after a project is completed, even if they were not the original builders. According to internal agency data, the previous policy forced property owners to spend more than $112 million in accessibility retrofits over the last five years just to qualify for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) refinancing—costs that HUD says directly choked off affordable housing supply. The rule eliminates the ability to hold current property owners indefinitely liable for architectural deviations committed by original builders decades in the past. Under the updated enforcement framework, the clock for filing Fair Housing Act design and construction challenges begins on the exact date a building receives its official certificate of occupancy. ONE UNEXPECTED PRICE SURGE MOST AMERICANS DON'T SEE IS RAISING THE STAKES FOR TRUMP BEFORE NOVEMBER Individuals or advocacy groups now have a strict one-year deadline to file administrative complaints directly with HUD. For private civil lawsuits filed in federal court, the statute of limitations caps claims at two years from the completion of construction. Once those respective windows close, property owners are shielded from retroactive, building-wide liability for original architectural flaws, though individual tenants retain the right to seek reasonable modifications for their specific housing needs at any time under existing Fair Housing Act protections. "[The Obama-era regulation] dramatically expanded the scope of the Fair Housing Act by declaring that deviations from HUD’s accessibility guidelines, at the point of initial construction, gave rise to strict liability against the builder in perpetuity," the new guidance says. "That interpretation was egregiously wrong. It exceeded the Department’s statutory authority, failed to increase the supply of accessible housing for individuals with disabilities, and imposed an unwarranted and unduly prejudicial burden on American homebuilders." According to internal transaction data and industry reports provided to HUD, the financial toll of the previous policy extended far beyond standard compliance fees typically associated with federally-backed refinancing. For example, a single third-party housing inspection firm identified nearly $49 million in required accessibility fixes across almost 500 refinance deals since 2019—averaging over $100,000 in deficiencies per property. Industry insiders and lenders also report that the Obama-era rules severely choked off financing, with one major affordable multifamily lender attributing more than $1 billion in lost HUD-insured loan volume over the last four years to the guidance, according to internal HUD data. Lenders told the agency that the ongoing uncertainty triggered recurring deal dropouts and discouraged prospective borrowers from pursuing FHA financing altogether. NEWSOM TARGETS MAJOR AFFORDABILITY SQUEEZE IN 'STRIKING' CONVERGENCE WITH TRUMP "For too long, unnecessary government policies have contributed to the skyrocketing cost of building, buying, and renting a home. Today’s action rescinds unnecessary and expensive liability created by legal theories that have no basis in law," said HUD Secretary Scott Turner. "The Trump Administration is following the law as written by Congress and interpreted by the courts. We will continue to repeal and replace guidance that does not honor these lawful commitments while ensuring Americans can access affordable housing." At the heart of the administration’s rollback is a fundamental legal principle that federal agencies cannot rewrite laws passed by lawmakers, nor can they ignore rulings by federal judges. When Congress updated the Fair Housing Act in 1988, lawmakers built in a strict one-year deadline to file administrative complaints. HUD officials argue the 2013 Obama-era policy effectively ignored that congressional mandate by allowing property owners to be targeted decades after a project was completed. The shift also aligns federal enforcement with appellate court rulings, including a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. Judges in that case ruled that the illegal act of failing to properly design a building ends when construction wraps up and an official certificate of occupancy is issued. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "Congress wrote a clear statute of limitations into the Fair Housing Act. That limitation is part of the law, not a suggestion for sly bureaucrats to disregard," said Assistant Secretary for Fair Housing and Equal Opportunity Craig Trainor. "We will not allow Obama-era guidance to rewrite the Fair Housing Act, expose American builders to indefinite legal liability, and make housing less affordable for hardworking American families."

articles.title: Ty Cobb: White House ‘turning into some combination of a whorehouse and Las Vegas’
articles.summary: Former White House lawyer Ty Cobb tore into President Trump’s White House ballroom project on Monday, saying the historic building is turning into a “combination of a whorehouse and Las Vegas.” Cobb, who served in the White House during Trump’s first term, made the comment hours after the Supreme Court cleared the way for construction…
articles.body:
Former White House lawyer Ty Cobb tore into President Trump’s White House ballroom project on Monday, saying the historic building is turning into a “combination of a whorehouse and Las Vegas.”

Cobb, who served in the White House during Trump’s first term, made the comment hours after the Supreme Court cleared the way for construction to continue on the planned ballroom.

“It certainly touched me because, as somebody who had spent a lot of time in the White House and in or about the grounds, you know, it was a beautiful setting and a historic setting,” Cobb said on CNN’s “OutFront.”

“It’s turning into some combination of a whorehouse and Las Vegas at this stage of the game with all the golden paving of it,” he continued. “It’s tragic what’s going on. But sadly, it’s going to continue, at least for the time being.”

In a 5-4 ruling on Monday, the Supreme Court halted a lower court ruling that blocked construction until Congress made additional approvals.

Chief Justice John Roberts sided with the court’s three liberals in opposing the decision, while five of the court’s conservative justices sided with the president.

“The White House is not just any building,” Roberts wrote in his dissent, adding that its “symbolism and history are wrapped up in its architecture.”

The five other conservative justices, three of which were appointed by Trump, ruled that the National Trust for Historic Preservation likely lacked standing to challenge the project.

The ruling does not settle whether Trump has the legal authority to build the ballroom, and the case could eventually return to the Supreme Court.

Trump celebrated Monday’s ruling, writing on Truth Social that the project is “under budget and ahead of schedule” and predicting the ballroom and accompanying military complex would be something “the entire Country is very proud of.”

“We are living in the Golden Age of America, and this Building will be one of the Greatest ever constructed in Washington, D.C.,” he wrote.

Trump demolished the East Wing last fall to make way for the 90,000-square-foot ballroom and has taken a hands-on role in the project.

articles.title: Trump approval stuck at lowest level of political career: Survey
articles.summary: President Trump’s approval rating has remained stagnant at the lowest point between his two presidencies, according to a new poll. The latest Reuters/Ipsos survey shows that Trump’s approval rating has remained at 33 percent — the third time the pollsters have found this result — amid the unpopularity of the Iran war and rising prices.…
articles.body:
President Trump’s approval rating has remained stagnant at the lowest point between his two presidencies, according to a new poll.

The latest Reuters/Ipsos survey shows that Trump’s approval rating has remained at 33 percent — the third time the pollsters have found this result — amid the unpopularity of the Iran war and rising prices .

His disapproval rating fell slightly from its highest point in his second term, down 2 points to 63 percent, the data shows.

The same poll found that 71 percent of respondents said they do not approve of Trump’s handling of the cost of living, which has become one of the top issues for voters during this primary election season and beyond. Pollsters found that 22 percent of respondents approved of his handling of the issue.

A plurality of voters, at 47 percent, said the cost of living would be the most important factor in deciding whom to support in November.

Registered Democrats in the survey appeared to be more likely to vote in the midterms than Republicans, with 46 percent of Democrats and 31 percent of Republicans saying they were “very enthusiastic” to cast a ballot. Independents preferred Democrats, at 36 percent, to win if the election was held today compared with 22 percent who said they would vote Republican.

The numbers follow what has been a tough summer for the president’s approval ratings, with other recent polling showing his approval dipping to 33 percent. The Decision Desk HQ approval average for the president hit 38.6 percent on Tuesday, a 1.5-point drop from last week.

Another recent poll showed his support sinking even further. The University of Massachusetts Amherst found that 32 percent of 1,000 respondents approved of his job performance, and 64 percent said they disapprove, including 54 percent who said they “strongly” disapprove.

When asked by The Hill last week to comment on the ratings, a White House official referred to a Truth Social post where the president claimed these polls were “Demoralization Operations” to discourage Republicans from voting and said real polls show him with stronger numbers, though he did not cite specific data.

The Reuters/Ipsos survey was conducted Aug. 28-31 and included 1,167 respondents. The margin of error is 3 percentage points.

articles.body:
GOP Rep. Tim Burchett (Tenn.) responded on Monday to President Trump’s statement that communities that oppose data center construction want to “ end up being backwards and poor .”

“I guess I’m backwards and poor,” he told MeidasTouch’s Pablo Manríquez on the House steps.

The Tennessee Republican suggested data centers could be built in military installations instead of in communities.

“We need more local control. We should have brought everybody to the table,” he added.

In a Truth Social post on Monday, the president encouraged Americans to welcome data center projects and “let Data Reign.”

“The good news is that there are plenty of other places that want them,” he wrote. “If we kill the Golden Goose, you will only have yourselves to blame.”

“China could not be happier with this anti Data Center movement,” he added.

House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) also suggested China was behind the growing skepticism about data centers in America.

“This is a competition with China. Let’s be clear about this,” Scalise told Fox News on Tuesday.

He added that the GOP is “investigating whether China is behind a lot of this misinformation, false information against data centers.”

In a Fox News poll conducted last month, 70 percent of respondents expressed opposition to the construction of a data center in their area, including 60 percent of Republicans and 76 percent of Democrats. Critics of these projects cite environmental and financial strains on the communities they are built in.

Some Republican state leaders have come out in favor of placing additional guardrails on data centers.

Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R), who had previously declared his state as the “epicenter of AI development,” recently issued a moratorium on new data center construction over concerns about water usage and power grid strains.

In an interview with ABC News’s “This Week” on Sunday, Abbott defended his reversal on this issue.

“They pop up in places that nobody ever heard of before, until they started the construction,” the Republican governor said. “And so, they had not been working in collaboration with the state, they’d not been in collaboration with local governments, and so they basically dug their own grave for the problem that’s been caused for them and that’s why they got the backlash they deserve.”

GOP Rep. Thomas Massie (Ky.), a frequent critic of the president and his administration’s policies, accused the companies behind data center projects of being “insensitive” in their placement.

“I don’t think you should let data reign without any kind of regulation at the local level,” he told Fox News. “You definitely need to let local people decide these things.”

articles.title: Roy Cohn is still up to his same old tricks
articles.summary: An op-ed by Bill Press argues that President Donald Trump’s political and legal strategies directly mirror the unethical tactics and principles of his late mentor, lawyer Roy Cohn.
articles.body:
Reincarnation has never been one of my core beliefs. Not until I read a gripping new book by noted biographer Kai Bird and his wife Susan Goldmark: “American Scoundrel: Roy Cohn’s Dark Journey from Joe McCarthy to Donald Trump.”

Now I am convinced that Roy Cohn didn’t die in 1986. He was simply reincarnated and is now president. President Trump is Roy Cohn incarnate.

Cohn was one of the most consequential figures of the 20th century, whose influence in the 21st century is as strong as ever. That doesn’t mean he was one of the most likeable. In fact, the portrait of Cohn painted by Bird and Goldmark is pure evil. It’s fascinating reading, but I felt like I needed to take a shower at the end of every chapter. From serving as Sen. Joe McCarthy’s (R-Wis.) pit bull during the Army-McCarthy hearings in 1954 to representing mafia dons in New York and Las Vegas, Cohn gained a reputation as a ruthless, unscrupulous, amoral, rule-breaking, judge-busting attorney who would lie, cheat, and steal to serve his clients and then brag about getting away with it — until he was finally disbarred in 1986.

Cohn met his most famous client in October 1973, when Trump and his father had been sued by the Justice Department for refusing to rent apartments to Black families. “What do you think we should do?” Trump asked. Cohn’s response was classic: “Tell them to go to hell and fight the thing in court and let them prove you discriminated.” Trump hired Cohn on the spot and went on to become his most loyal disciple, not only following Cohn’s advice, but adopting and practicing his unethical tactics — which he still does today.

Indeed, the big take-away from “American Scoundrel” is how closely Trump’s actions reflect and repeat lessons he learned from Roy Cohn, all founded on what the New York Times called Cohn’s three rules: “1. Never settle, never surrender. 2. Counterattack, counter-sue immediately. 3. No matter what happens, no matter how deeply into the muck you get, claim victory and never admit defeat.”

In conducting his business or dealing with adversaries, everything Trump does he learned from Roy Cohn, starting with the least serious. Under Cohn’s tutelage, McCarthy delighted in giving his critics denigrating nicknames. Sen. Stuart Symington (D-Mo.) became “Sanctimonious Stu.” Sen. Margaret Chase Smith (R-Maine) was “Snow White.” For Trump, Rep. Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) was “Crazy Nancy.” Joe Biden was “Sleepy Joe.”

“Another lesson Trump learned from Cohn,” note Bird and Goldmark, “was his cavalier attitude toward paying his bills.” He stiffed restaurants, contractors, business partners, travel agencies and the IRS. Like his mentor, Trump soon gained a reputation for being a celebrity cheapskate. In 2016, USA Today reported at least 60 lawsuits by painters, plumbers, cabinet makers, waiters, bartenders, and lawyers who said Trump failed to pay them.

On a much more serious scale, Cohn taught Trump not to let facts get in the way. Cohn and McCarthy convinced the country of a “Red Scare” when, in fact, there were only 25,000 members of the American Communist Party in 1953. As New York Times columnist Tony Lewis wrote, “The Communist threat inside the United States was minuscule, if it existed at all.” And, of course, Trump never bothers about facts in claiming he won the popular vote in 2016 , he actually won the election in 2020, and those who stormed the Capitol on Jan. 6 were “patriots.”

When one of his clients was unhappy with what was printed about them, Cohn would tell them to sue the newspaper. Following that advice to the letter, Trump has sued ABC, CBS, CNN, BBC, the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal, and the Washington Post — all because he didn’t like what they reported.

Of course, Trump lives by Cohn’s cardinal rule of when attacked, counter-attack. Cohn would be proud of how Trump has used the Justice Department to pursue dozens of perceived political opponents, including former FBI Director James Comey, New York Attorney General Letitia James, former National Security Adviser John Bolton, former CIA Director John Brennan, and several members of Congress. And, once in court, Trump follows Cohn’s other rule: delay, delay, delay.

Of all lessons Trump learned from Cohn, the only one I cannot confirm is Cohn’s well-documented habit of picking up a fork and eating from other peoples’ plates in restaurants . But the next time I dine at Mar-a-Lago, I’ll let you know.

articles.title: Ex-House Freedom Caucus chair says GOP isn't 'a conservative party anymore,' but Democrats are 'worse'
articles.summary: Former Rep. Bob Good, former chair of the House Freedom Caucus, indicated that the Republican Party is not "a conservative party anymore."
articles.body: Former Rep. Bob Good, who chaired the House Freedom Caucus during part of his congressional tenure, recently told Fox News Digital that the GOP is not, based on "any standard of measurement, a conservative party anymore." "Republicans have kind of been Democrat-lite in their policies" for "nearly two years," Good, who lost a 2024 GOP U.S. House primary in Virginia to a challenger backed by then-former President Donald Trump, told Fox News Digital during an interview on Friday. Republicans have held the majority in both chambers of Congress so far throughout Trump's second term. But Good suggested that during the last "year and a half, 19 months or so," they "have massively squandered the opportunity that was given to them by the voters." "We've taken the debt to $40 trillion. We've added new entitlement programs like Trump accounts," Good said. He pointed to "government taking ownership stakes in private companies," adding, "We haven't made the case for why we're in a war that's lasted over six months now." "The real emergency, the real crisis, is the debt crisis," Good asserted. FORMER FREEDOM CAUCUS CHAIR BOB GOOD BLASTS TRUMP'S ENDORSEMENT RECORD: 'TRUMP IS THE PROBLEM' Good argued that Trump does not discuss the debt issue "in a serious way." "I think he suspects that spending cuts and spending reforms aren't particularly popular," the former congressman told Fox News Digital. "And I think wants to be popular." Republican National Committee spokeswoman Emma Hall said in a statement to Fox News Digital on Monday, "President Trump and Republicans are delivering America First results every day — and it’s why we’ll defy history and win in November. No one is interested in advice from certified loser Bob Good." White House spokesman Kush Desai declared in a statement provided to Fox News Digital, "President Trump was given a resounding mandate by the American people to smash Washington, D.C.’s obsession with consensus orthodoxy that has let Americans down. The Trump administration is turning the page on Joe Biden’s economic disaster by implementing traditional free market policies that do work — like deregulation and tax cuts — while rectifying longtime America Last policies that have left Americans behind." Good said he thinks that turnout will represent the "primary challenge" for the GOP during the midterm elections. He opined that Republicans are running on not being "as bad as Democrats." "Keep the House cuz we're not as bad as Democrats is not a truly inspirational motivating factor," Good noted. US ECONOMY 'WORSE' OFF THAN WHEN BIDEN DEPARTED, PETER SCHIFF SAYS, WARNING OF 2028 DEM SOCIALIST 'THREAT' Good indicated that the GOP should have drastically downsized government last year. "What they should have done in year one, in 2025, was to massively cut spending, massively shrink government, massively implement spending reforms, go for broke while they had the power before it was an election year, and then the American people I think would've rewarded them... with midterm victory," he said. He expressed hope that Republicans could perform well due to redistricting, as well as "because Democrat policies are so unpopular, and Democrat candidates are so extreme." And despite his criticisms of Republicans, Good asserts that "the Democrats are certainly worse." "President Trump has done a lot of great things. President Trump immediately secured the border, to such degree, it's not even talked about anymore," he said. FORMER FREEDOM CAUCUS CHAIR BOB GOOD CALLS OUT 'THE BIG GLARING WEAKNESS FOR ALL OF REPUBLICAN GOVERNMENT CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Good pointed to other issues such as Trump's efforts to cut regulations and taxes, and to target diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) ideology in the federal government and education. "Democrats would do none of those things," Good said, adding that every area in which "the Republicans have failed or been benign or weak or tepid or not followed through, Democrats would be even worse."

articles.title: We cannot go back on Medicaid coverage for people living with HIV
articles.summary: HIV can be a fatal disease if access to comprehensive care and treatment is interrupted or unavailable.
articles.body:
As an infectious diseases physician who provides HIV care in Kentucky, I often see the serious health consequences of patients going without health insurance.

Not long ago, a young adult man was transferred to my hospital after eight months of rapidly declining health, including neurologic issues, significant weight loss, high fever, shortness of breath and confusion. Uninsured, and after months of fragmented and inconsistent care, he was diagnosed at our hospital with advanced HIV.

More than 1.2 million people are living with HIV in the U.S. Around 38,000 are newly diagnosed every year, and 22 percent of them, like my patient, are diagnosed late in the course of the disease after their immune system has been severely impaired .

Uninterrupted access to HIV treatment suppresses the virus to undetectable levels, protecting the immune system and stopping HIV transmission . Virally suppressed patients can stay healthy and do not transmit HIV. Yet only 69 percent of people diagnosed with HIV in the U.S. are virally suppressed and benefiting from HIV treatment.

HIV can be a fatal disease if access to comprehensive care and treatment is interrupted or unavailable. Healthcare, including antiretroviral therapy, involves at least twice-yearly medical appointments and laboratory monitoring. For some, substance use and mental health treatment, as well as treatment for other conditions common among people with HIV (diabetes, cardiovascular disease and cancer) is necessary.

Prior to the Affordable Care Act and the Medicaid expansion, 40 percent of my patients were uninsured. Twelve years later, that number had dropped to 10 percent, approaching the national rate of 8 percent . Nationally, nearly 50 percent of people with HIV now have Medicaid coverage.

Before the Affordable Care Act, our largely employer-based healthcare system excluded most people with HIV from health coverage due to pre-existing conditions and other insurer practices. The primary pathway to Medicaid for low-income people with HIV was through the Social Security Insurance Program , which required them to be disabled in addition to having very limited or no income.

When Medicaid expansion launched in 2014 in my state and others that adopted it , there were tears of relief. My uninsured patients for the first time had access to health insurance offering reliable coverage for the comprehensive care their lives depend on.

Now that coverage is at risk. The 2025 H.R. 1 legislation requires most Medicaid expansion enrollees between ages 19 and 64 to complete and report at least 80 hours of work or “community engagement” activities per month beginning Jan. 1, 2027. Recognizing the importance of health coverage to certain populations, H.R. 1 included an exclusion from the requirements for people with serious or complex conditions that did not require disability or impairment.

Unfortunately, though, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services appear to have abandoned that exclusion. The center’s interim final rule implementing the work requirements stipulates that people with HIV and other serious or complex conditions must be seriously impaired by their condition to qualify for the exclusion.

Although requiring Medicaid expansion enrollees to work and regularly report work or community engagement hours may seem simple, it does not reflect the reality of my patients’ lives. Navigating administrative hurdles to access healthcare can be challenging for any of us. These bureaucratic challenges are magnified for my patients, who live on low incomes and often lack transportation or home access to the internet, personal computers or smart phones. Their health can rapidly deteriorate if they miss medical appointments or are unable to fill a prescription.

Every day, I see the consequences of medical red tape and how missing deadlines can lead to months of interrupted HIV therapy that can result in permanent harm to the immune system or death. These logistical obstacles are also costly for our clinic. Nearly 40 percent of our patients have Medicaid, 90 percent of whom require help every six months filing paperwork to maintain their health coverage. The new requirements will place additional strain on medical teams who are already managing significant workloads.

And to what end? Several states have already experimented with work requirements. One state, Arkansas , saw increases in uninsured rates but not in employment.

Whereas my patient’s late HIV diagnosis highlights the broken parts of our healthcare system, the Medicaid expansion has for more than a decade demonstrated what works, providing affordable health coverage to people with low incomes and improving their health and the health of our communities .

Reliable access to healthcare is a necessity for people with HIV and others with serious or complex conditions. After seeing what a difference the Medicaid expansion has made, my hope is that policymakers will not roll back progress by allowing red tape to take away this lifeline from their most vulnerable constituents.

Alice Thornton, M.D., FIDSA, is vice chair of the HIV Medicine Association.

(Jesus Aranguren/AP Images for AIDS Healthcare Foundation)

articles.title: Trump calls on Congress to pass film and TV tax incentive
articles.summary: President Trump urged Congress on Monday evening to “immediately” approve federal tax incentives for movie and TV production. In a Truth Social post, the president said he had met earlier in the day with actor Jon Voight and that the pair discussed the movement of film industry jobs out of the U.S. to other countries. …
articles.body:
President Trump urged Congress on Monday evening to “immediately” approve federal tax incentives for movie and TV production.

In a Truth Social post , the president said he had met earlier in the day with actor Jon Voight and that the pair discussed the movement of film industry jobs out of the U.S. to other countries.

“Jon, and many others in the Industry, are suggesting we do Federal Tax Incentives in order to Make our Movie and Television Production Business GREAT AGAIN, perhaps GREATER THAN EVER BEFORE!” Trump wrote, adding that meetings on this issue are being scheduled with “Leaders of both Parties.”

“It should be Bipartisan, especially since so much money is being lost in California, and other largely Blue States,” the president continued. “I am going to suggest that Republicans and Democrats get together, and immediately craft Legislation to save the Movie, Television, and Entertainment Business in America.”

Major U.S. film hubs like Los Angeles have lost movie and TV production to countries like Canada due to rising production costs and taxes.

“There is no incentive to be there, and it is hurting California very badly,” Trump wrote in his Monday post, referring to film production in the state of California.

A report released this year from Otis College of Art and Design found that California lost 14 percent of its creative jobs — most of which were concentrated in the film industry — between 2022 and 2025. The report’s authors cited a lack of funding for these roles and structural changes within this industry as the factors driving this change.

Democratic Sen. Adam Schiff (Calif.) supported the proposed tax incentives in a social media post on Monday, writing that he was “in strong agreement with the President” on this issue.

“Congress should immediately take up and pass a federal film tax incentive to bring back these good-paying jobs that we’ve lost to other countries,” Schiff wrote. “Let’s work together — Republicans and Democrats — to get this done, and bring the movie magic back to America.”

Nicki Minaj and actor Dean Cain are taking starring roles in a “Shark Tank”-style event being held by the Small Business Administration (SBA).

“Starships” rapper Minaj — who’s described herself as President Trump’s likely “No. 1 fan” — will join an “all-star judging panel” including Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia and investor Grant Cardone at the SBA’s “Million Dollar Pitch Competition” on Sep. 18, the agency announced this week.

Cain, who played the Man of Steel in the 1990’s series “Lois & Clark: The New Adventures of Superman,” will host the live event in Washington.

As part of the competition, “five successful entrepreneur finalists will pitch their small businesses for a chance to win a portion of a $1 million cash prize pool funded by Clover Network, Inc.,” according to the SBA.

The five national finalists poised to compete include Compotech Inc., Winton Machine, Plas-Tech Tooling, Red River and VetPowered. Prizes range from $75,000 for fifth place to $400,000 for the first-place winner.

SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler touted the match-up and its celeb-filled lineup, saying in a statement that Minaj, Cain and others will “only add to the excitement of this historic celebration of free enterprise.”

“Their presence will be invaluable in highlighting the unique and inspiring stories of the five finalists competing for $1 million in growth capital, and the importance of Main Street businesses in powering American strength,” Loeffler said.

The SBA said its pitch competition was created as part of Freedom 250, a public-private initiative launched by the Trump administration in 2025 to mark the country’s semiquincentennial birthday this year.

articles.title: Who is Alejandro Betancourt, ex-Chavez ally now Trump’s Venezuela oil man?
articles.summary: The controversial tycoon will lead the joint oil venture as the Trump administration seeks to reshape energy markets.
articles.body:
Controversial Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, who amassed massive fortunes under former socialist President Hugo Chavez and who has faced investigations into alleged money laundering, has been tapped by the Trump administration to lead a new US-backed oil venture in the Latin American nation.

On Friday, President Donald Trump announced that the US has reached a deal with Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez under which Washington will acquire majority control over more than 65 billion barrels’ worth of proven oil reserves.

As part of the deal, the US government plans to take a 35 percent passive stake in Betancourt’s North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) – Venezuela’s second-largest oil firm.

In a statement, Betancourt said Venezuela is “blessed with an abundance of natural resources, hardworking people and untapped potential”, adding that the deal will “unleash that potential to the great benefit of both Venezuelans and Americans”.

So who is Betancourt, 46, and why is Trump relying on him to tap into Venezuela’s oil sector?

Betancourt made fortunes after his firm, Derwick Associates, won contracts to build power plants under the government of President Chavez following an acute power crisis triggered by drought in the late 2000s.

Critics say the firm won those contracts often without bidding, earning billions of dollars. Betancourt and other firms, which received lucrative contracts during the Chavez era, are often called “bolichicos,” meaning the “Bolivarian boys”.

His net worth is believed to be $2.6bn, according to media reports.

But in 2017, anticorruption watchdog Transparencia Venezuela accused the company of inflating prices during the drought period.

In 2021, another report by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) said Betancourt was involved in corruption and money laundering networks linked to the Venezuelan state.

Over the past decade, he has faced money laundering investigations in the US, Spain and Switzerland. In 2025, the Venezuelan tycoon was arrested twice in the UK following extradition requests from Switzerland and Spain over alleged money laundering cases.

Betancourt, who has the experience of running oil fields in Venezuela, became a person of interest for the Trump administration, which has been looking to exploit the country’s vast oil resources.

This year, the US administration intervened in the Swiss investigations into Betancourt and urged ked the UK government to lift travel curbs on him, according to US media reports.

The Venezuelan businessman has denied the accusations and has faced no formal criminal charges or convictions.

Betancourt also leads the O’Hara administration, an international Spain-based investment group, where he serves as the president and one of the main shareholders of Hawkers, an e-commerce company that sells sunglasses.

Born into a wealthy family in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, Betancourt initially worked in the energy sector after completing a Master’s in Business Administration course from Oxford University in the United Kingdom.

In April 2024, he cofounded NABEP, and a year later, took full control of the company, which has its headquarters in Bridgetown, Barbados.

Why does Trump want to partner with Betancourt?

Trump’s control of Venezuelan oil comes amid upheaval in the global energy market due to the war on Iran, which has affected US energy security. Its reserves are at a record low. Earlier this week, Trump said that he will use the Venezuelan oil to fill the US oil reserves.

The joint venture with the NABEP, which produces about 200,000 barrels of crude oil per day, will help expand production, as Iran’s blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has spiked global oil prices, including in the US. The high energy prices will likely cost Trump politically in the November Midterm elections.

On Monday, the White House released a fact sheet, which says that the US is creating a private joint venture with North American Blue Energy Partners – which the Trump administration aims to use to gain a larger stake in Venezuela’s oil reserves.

Back in January, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio had accused the socialist government led by President Nicolas Maduro of creating a hub for China and Russia.

“This is our Hemisphere – and President Trump will not allow our security to be threatened,” Rubio said after the military operation in Caracas.

Venezuela holds approximately 17 percent of the world’s total oil reserves, but due to the US sanctions and mismanagement, it remains underdeveloped. The country currently produces about one million barrels of oil a day, which is just about 1 percent of global production.

Venezuela’s interim leader has welcomed the oil deal, which is expected to add the much-needed funds to the state’s treasury.

The association with the US will make it easy for NABEP to operate the Venezuelan economy, which still remains under US sanctions.

In a statement to the Reuters news agency, NABEP said, “Mr Betancourt has been in the Venezuelan oil industry for more than 15 years with a consistent track record of success, most recently at the helm of NABEP, where he rapidly scaled the company’s production.”

The company added that it has a near-term goal of increasing production to more than 1 million barrels of oil per day.

How will The US government investment in Betancourt’s venture take place?

According to the White House, in the latest deal with Venezuela, the Venezuelan interim authorities have granted NABEP “100-year concessions for 17 oil fields with proven reserves of approximately 65 billion barrels.” Many of those fields were previously owned by Russian or Chinese firms, the White House noted.

“NABEP has also developed an ambitious plan to rapidly scale production by investing up to $100 billion in new oil infrastructure in Venezuela, helping to drive economic growth, support thousands of high-paying jobs in Venezuela, and lead to tens of billions in broader economic activity,” the White House added.

Meanwhile, the deal will give the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital a 35 percent ownership stake in the company, the White House disclosed. The US will also be guaranteed a right to buy 20 percent of the output at cost, orchestrated through the State Department.

The agreement, which the White House said secures “our energy dominance for the next century”, was signed by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

On Friday, Trump had said that the deal “MORE THAN DOUBLES American Oil Reserves”.

But on Monday, he acknowledged that US consumers would not immediately see a change in petrol prices. Asked about a timeline at the White House, Trump said “it could be a little bit” for prices to fall, and he played down analyst predictions that it could take years.

“If it was two years, you know, that’s a short period of time,” he said.

articles.title: Whistleblower warns of potential Postal Service system failure for midterms
articles.summary: A whistleblower on Monday warned that the U.S. Postal Service’s computer system is riddled with errors and could jeopardize mail-in voting in the November midterm elections, according to a statement from Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.). The individual said the Postal Service has attempted to build a complex system over a three-month time frame, beginning on…
articles.body:
A whistleblower on Monday warned that the U.S. Postal Service’s computer system is riddled with errors and could jeopardize mail-in voting in the November midterm elections, according to a statement from Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.).

The individual said the Postal Service has attempted to build a complex system over a three-month time frame, beginning on or around June 15, to be used for the midterms, a process that typically takes a year or longer.

The work was expected to stop amid a federal judge’s ruling that temporarily halted President Trump’s executive order to limit voting by mail, a ruling that the Trump administration has appealed .

“The whistleblower’s allegations also provide disturbing information suggesting that USPS may have violated a court order by continuing to implement the EO despite being ordered to cease all such work,” Blumenthal wrote Monday in a letter to Postmaster General David Steiner.

“We urge you to abandon this ill-conceived, unconscionable plan and ensure that all Americans can exercise their constitutional right to vote, including by mail, without interference by USPS,” Blumenthal added.

The Hill has reached out to the Postal Service for comment.

Boston-based U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani barred Trump’s executive order last month, but the Supreme Court overruled her after its conservative majority determined the block was premature. But Talwani issued her ruling again after siding with a group of blue states and private voting rights groups that claimed the executive order’s effect on the Postal Service was unconstitutional.

The order introduces a portal for the Postal Service to screen ballots submitted by state election officials. But the whistleblower identified “deeply flawed plans” with the portal and called the portal’s development “rushed” and “risky and haphazard.”

The whistleblower said standard and needed testing had been eliminated and that it created “the substantial risk of a ‘catastrophic failure’ of the system that could ‘derail the midterm elections,'” Blumenthal said, quoting the whistleblower.

“Without clear guidance, ‘[d]ifferent team members continued to have different understandings of how the system is supposed to function which caused ongoing and greater confusion among the group,’ substantially increasing the risk that the system will fail and, ultimately, disenfranchise voters,” the Connecticut Democrat wrote, again quoting the whistleblower.

Blumenthal called on Steiner to answer several questions from the Homeland Security Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, on which Blumenthal serves as the ranking member. He called the Postal Service’s plans a “seemingly illegal plot to interfere in November’s midterms.”

Questions included when Postal Service employees and contractors were told to develop the new portal, whether there will be beta testing for the portal, how long it will take to remedy false positives, whether or not the Postal Service has communicated with state officials about the portal and any records or communications about the date for when the portal would be completed, among other questions.

“Their system is set up to fail – and risk the right to vote for millions of Americans who cast their ballots by mail,” Blumenthal said in a statement. “Given this new information, such sloppiness and haste seems clearly part of a purposeful attempt to create chaos and prevent people from voting. I am demanding answers and accountability.”

The group Whistleblower Aid said in its summary of the whistleblower’s statement that the goal was to have the portal active on Tuesday. They called the process “sloppy” and said that it “poses significant risk.”

“Potentially millions of American voters may not receive their mail-in ballot this election cycle in a timely manner, or at all,” Whistleblower Aid wrote. “The whistleblower’s assessment and recitation of the facts around the risky and haphazard development of the project is a compelling warning of catastrophic failure which could derail the midterm elections.”

The order follows years of unfounded claims made by the president, who claims that mail-in voting causes widespread voting discrepancies and is used to “rig” elections without substantial evidence.

articles.body: Las acusaciones de Pedro Sánchez sobre la supuesta utilización de la crisis migratoria de Ceuta para desestabilizar a España han provocado nuevas reacciones en redes sociales. La cuenta de Anonymous @YourAnonCentral ha respaldado públicamente las palabras del presidente del Gobierno y ha señalado a Rusia e Israel, además de a sectores de la extrema derecha internacional, como responsables de campañas destinadas a atacar la posición de España. El mensaje publicado por la cuenta de Anonymous es el siguiente: “Si más líderes europeos hablaran la verdad como Sánchez, entonces tal vez Francia y Alemania no estarían a punto de ser entregadas a manos rusas / sionistas” Sánchez aseguró que Rusia, Israel y una “internacional ultraderechista” habían contribuido a difundir bulos y desinformación en torno a la crisis migratoria de Ceuta. El Gobierno sostiene que sus declaraciones se apoyan, entre otros elementos, en información procedente del Servicio Europeo de Acción Exterior. La reacción de Moscú no se ha hecho esperar. Rusia ha rechazado las acusaciones y ha exigido al Gobierno español que presente pruebas que demuestren su implicación. La portavoz del Ministerio de Exteriores ruso, María Zajárova, ha criticado que Sánchez haya realizado estas afirmaciones públicamente en lugar de recurrir a los canales diplomáticos correspondientes. Por su parte, Israel también ha negado cualquier responsabilidad en la crisis. Mientras tanto, la Comisión Europea ha confirmado que existe un informe que identifica campañas de desinformación de origen ruso relacionadas con los acontecimientos de Ceuta. No obstante, Bruselas ha precisado que esas campañas fueron detectadas después de la entrada masiva de migrantes y no ha confirmado públicamente una participación israelí. El mensaje de Anonymous llega en un momento de plena polémica política y diplomática. La cuenta considera que las declaraciones de Sánchez refuerzan su teoría inicial, aunque las acusaciones más amplias sobre una actuación coordinada entre Rusia, Israel, Estados Unidos y grupos ultraderechistas continúan sin estar probadas.

articles.title: Haberman: ‘No polling’ where Trump is popular
articles.summary: CNN political analyst Maggie Haberman said Monday that President Trump’s approval is sinking across nearly all polls as the midterm elections near. “There is no polling where this president is popular. Let’s put it that way,” Haberman said during an appearance on CNN’s “The Source” with Kaitlan Collins. “And there is no polling where he…
articles.body:
CNN political analyst Maggie Haberman said Monday that President Trump’s approval is sinking across nearly all polls as the midterm elections near.

“There is no polling where this president is popular. Let’s put it that way,” Haberman said during an appearance on CNN’s “The Source” with Kaitlan Collins.

“And there is no polling where he is not in trouble on the issue of affordability,” she added.

Collins had pointed to new CNN polling showing Trump with a net approval rating of negative 32 percentage points, compared with negative 21 points for the Republican Party overall.

New polling shows Trump’s approval rating has dipped to its lowest point between his two terms in office as the widely unpopular Iran war stretches into its sixth month and Americans remain concerned over rising prices .

Haberman, a reporter for The New York Times, cautioned that public surveys do not always line up with private polling she has seen, but said the broader picture remains difficult for Trump, particularly on the cost of living.

She pointed to an Oval Office event on healthcare earlier Monday, where administration officials repeatedly invoked “affordability” — an issue Trump has previously dismissed as a “hoax” perpetuated by Democrats.

“That is the kind of thing that Republicans who are in these districts that are embattled do not want to be dealing with,” Haberman said.

Trump and GOP leadership have sought to make the president a central figure in the party’s midterm strategy despite his weak approval ratings, in an effort to secure votes from his base.

The president urged voters ahead of the midterms to pretend he is “on the ballot” when they cast their votes in November, as the party looks to ramp up voter turnout.

Trump has publicly clashed with Haberman in the past over her coverage of his presidency, calling the Times reporter “Maggot Haberman” on several occasions during his critique of her writing.

He recently lashed out at her over a story about his plans for the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, where she and three other Times journalists reported that Trump plans to skip a ceremony in New York City commemorating the anniversary and instead attend the Irish Open after event organizers denied his request to speak.

Speeches from politicians at the ceremony have been banned by the National September 11 Memorial and Museum since 2012.

“She’s been falsely writing about me for years — She’s a stalker, and should be forced to turn over any and all money that she’s made through her fake reporting on me,” Trump wrote of Haberman.

Trump is expected to attend a memorial service at the Pentagon this month on the anniversary of the attack, and Vice President Vance will represent the White House at the New York event, according to the Times.

articles.title: Bessent: Iran economy could collapse ‘within weeks or months’
articles.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday said Iran’s economy could collapse “within weeks or months,” as the Trump administration seeks to debilitate the Middle Eastern country’s economy. “I think it could be within weeks or months –– and the economy doesn’t have to collapse, we just have to have the regime come to their senses,”…
articles.body:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday said Iran’s economy could collapse “within weeks or months,” as the Trump administration seeks to debilitate the Middle Eastern country’s economy.

“I think it could be within weeks or months –– and the economy doesn’t have to collapse, we just have to have the regime come to their senses,” he told reporters when asked how long it would take for the Iranian economy to collapse.

He added that the latest sanctions, as part of what the Trump administration has called an “economic D-Day,” are backed by the European Union, saying the U.S. has its “fulsome support.” The EU said Sunday that it was working with the U.S. and other partners to put pressure on Iran’s economy.

Bessent told The Associated Press in an interview on Sunday that the U.S. will sanction another Iranian bank as part of this pressure campaign, called Operation Economic Outcast. The secretary noted that the Trump administration is prepared to instill “financial violence if we have to.”

The remarks came before and after a Monday meeting with Bessent and the Group of 20 finance ministers in Asheville, N.C., where he said he wanted to focus on growing the world economy.

Bessent and President Trump, along with other Cabinet members, have reached out to their counterparts in other countries to urge them to sever their financial ties with Iran or face consequences.

The Treasury secretary also warned that “all options are on the table” to sanction China for continuing to purchase Iranian oil.

The president has so far not followed through with the economic warfare approach, but both sides exchanged fire at one another on Sunday and Monday in the first known attacks by U.S. and Iranian forces since late last month.

The two countries have been locked in a stalemate over control of the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran has kept closed off to commercial vessels exporting what amounts to one-fifth of the world’s oil. Trump responded with a U.S. naval blockade deployed outside Iranian ports in the strait.

Closing the strait has led to soaring gas prices, with the national average in the U.S. reaching $4.10 per gallon on Tuesday, nearly $1 more than the average at this time last year, according to AAA’s data . Crude oil also jumped more than 3 percent following the strikes, with futures for Brent crude , the international benchmark, at $92.50 per barrel and futures for the North American standard, West Texas Intermediate , at $88 per barrel.

Trump has downplayed concerns over gas prices, defending the choice to take military action against Iran to prevent it from developing or obtaining a nuclear weapon. But his administration has released oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) to fight back against these high costs, resulting in the SPR reaching its lowest level since 1983 .

The president on Sunday said that following an oil deal reached with the Venezuelan government to control more than 65 billion barrels of oil from the South American country, the U.S. will be able to “fill up” the SPR .

articles.title: Jury in Lindsay Clancy trial can’t get a unanimous decision, judge says to keep deliberating
articles.summary: Coming near the start of the fourth day of deliberations, this was the first time the jury gave any indication they were at an impasse.
articles.body:
EDITOR’S NOTE: This story includes discussion of suicide. If you or someone you know needs help, the national suicide and crisis lifeline in the U.S. is available by calling or texting 988.

PLYMOUTH, Mass. (AP) — Jurors in the Lindsay Clancy trial said Tuesday they’ve been unable to reach a unanimous decision on whether the Massachusetts mother was criminally responsible for killing her three young children , but the judge told them to keep trying.

The jury is in its fourth day of deliberations in what has been a closely watched trial focused on maternal mental health after childbirth, and which has stirred deep divisions among the public.

This was the first time the jury gave any indication they were at an impasse. Clancy stared straight ahead as the jury entered, then looked toward them as the judge spoke to the panel.

“I know that this was a long trial, all right,” Judge William Sullivan said. “I know there were over 80 witnesses. There were over 300 exhibits. But because of that, I’m going to ask you to go back out.”

Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse, doesn’t deny strangling her children but says postpartum psychosis led to her actions. Prosecutors argue she knew what she was doing. Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty by reason of lack of criminal responsibility.

The jury could convict her of murder or manslaughter, or acquit her if jurors believe her deteriorating mental health was to blame. A conviction could lead to a life prison sentence. If she is acquitted, a judge could still order her confined to a mental health facility if an evaluation determines she is a danger to the public.

If the jurors can’t reach a verdict and a mistrial is declared, the charges against Clancy would remain and prosecutors would need to decide whether to try Clancy again.

The jury began deliberating on Thursday afternoon. On Friday, they asked to look at a knife that Clancy used to cut herself shortly after the killings, and bags with empty prescription pill bottles found in her house.

During more than four weeks of testimony, jurors heard differing views from medical experts about Clancy’s mental state after the birth of her third child, as well as her culpability.

Clancy’s lawyer argued she loved her children , but killed them because she lost her grip on reality — and on herself — due to postpartum psychosis, a rare mental illness that can follow childbirth.

Both Clancy’s mother and sister testified that she became anxious, paranoid and suicidal. Clancy sought treatment for her worsening mental health, including a stay in a psychiatric hospital, in the months before killing Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy, ages 5, 3 and 8 months.

Less than three weeks after being discharged, she sent her husband out on an errand and killed the children with exercise bands in the basement of their home south of Boston. She then jumped from a second-floor window and remains paralyzed from the waist down.

Prosecutors said Clancy was depressed and tired of living , and made a conscious choice to kill the children before attempting suicide. A forensic psychologist who testified for the prosecution said he concluded that Clancy killed the children because she wanted to end her life but didn’t want to leave them behind.

According to her defense, she had bipolar disorder and postpartum psychosis that, ultimately, led her to believe she heard a voice telling her to kill the children so she could end her own life. A psychologist who took the stand for the defense said Clancy didn’t recognize the “wrongfulness” of killing her children because of her mental health issues.

Clancy chose not to testify. She watched the proceedings from the defense table, occasionally weeping , as when prosecutors showed autopsy photos of the children to the jury.

Jurors also spent two days listening to testimony from her former husband, Patrick Clancy, and his anguished 911 call . He was still on the phone when he discovered the children’s bodies, minutes after finding his wife badly injured in the yard.

Patrick Clancy has said in interviews that he forgives his ex-wife, whom he viewed as ill rather than evil. The trial marks the first time he has seen Lindsay Clancy since the killings.

Postpartum psychosis, the condition that Clancy’s attorney says she had when she killed the children, is more serious and less common than postpartum depression.

Researchers estimate that the condition afflicts 1 to 2 out of 1,000 women after delivery. Although most who develop it don’t harm their children, mothers with severe cases might try to harm themselves or their kids.

articles.title: House Democrats demand answers over ICE’s $16.7M purchase of 6,000 electric shock gloves
articles.summary: Democrats on the House Committee on Homeland Security on Monday expressed their “strong opposition” to the Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) plans to spend up to $20 million on electric shock gloves for their agents. ICE awarded a $16.7 million contract with Compliant Technologies LLC for 6,000 of the company’s Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter…
articles.body:
Democrats on the House Committee on Homeland Security on Monday expressed their “strong opposition” to the Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) plans to spend up to $20 million on electric shock gloves for their agents.

ICE awarded a $16.7 million contract with Compliant Technologies LLC for 6,000 of the company’s Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter (G.L.O.V.E.) product, according to a funding notice published last month.

The Homeland Democrats pointed to past incidents of ICE using violent force during immigration enforcement operations in a letter to ICE’s acting director, David Venturella. They cited The New York Times’ reporting that agents have shot at least 23 people and killed six others since last year.

“We have many questions about ICE’s nearly $17 million contract for a device that is likely to be incorrectly used or abused by officers and agents resulting in more violence, injury or deaths,” they wrote.

The lawmakers included Democratic Reps. Lou Correa (Calif.), Shri Thanedar (Mich.), Seth Magaziner (R.I.), Dan Goldman (N.Y.), Timothy Kennedy (N.Y.), LaMonica McIver (N.J.), Julie Johnson (Texas) and Pablo José Hernández (P.R.).

Local law enforcement agencies, such as the Oklahoma County Jail, have used this technology, according to Oklahoma outlet KFOR . The device acts like a taser with a lower voltage level.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, pushed back against these concerns in a statement to The Hill.

“Congressional Democrats have made it clear that they no longer support the brave men and women of ICE, and the inflammatory rhetoric they and their allies have levied against them has led to unprecedented levels of threats and assaults,” the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson added that federal officers are “highly trained in de-escalation tactics and regularly receive ongoing use of force training.”

The House Democrats’ request follows a letter last week from a group of Democratic senators to Venturella, in which the lawmakers expressed “deep concern” with this planned purchase.

“Over the past year, ICE personnel has been involved in numerous well-documented incidents of excessive force and civil rights violations,” the senators wrote. “These incidents have shown the American people that ICE personnel are not adequately trained or accountable for their interactions with civilians.”

ICE is also planning to spend up to $2 million on robot “dogs” to assist their agents with immigration operations, according to a funding document posted on Thursday.

These robots, which are equipped with cameras and chemical detectors, will be used as “an additional tool to safely assess potentially dangerous situations” before deploying officers to a scene, an ICE spokesperson told The Hill.

“This technology does not replace law enforcement officers or their judgement — it simply provides another option to help protect officers and the communities they serve,” the spokesperson said.

articles.summary: President Trump’s secret departure on an alternate military aircraft over the summer in Turkey is getting the Netflix documentary treatment. “Instadocs: The Decoy Plane,” premiering Friday on the streamer, will explore how the president was secretly shuttled inside a catering truck to a smaller Air Force C-32A plane in July amid security concerns involving Iran. The documentary…
articles.body:
President Trump’s secret departure on an alternate military aircraft over the summer in Turkey is getting the Netflix documentary treatment.

“Instadocs: The Decoy Plane,” premiering Friday on the streamer, will explore how the president was secretly shuttled inside a catering truck to a smaller Air Force C-32A plane in July amid security concerns involving Iran.

The documentary will detail the story “through the eyes of the traveling press corps with firsthand accounts” from journalists including Associated Press White House photographer Alex Brandon and The Washington Post’s Dan Lamothe, among others, Netflix said in a Tuesday announcement about the project.

“As we get on the tarmac, and we round and I look at Air Force One, I see those catering vehicles up against the side of Air Force One. There’s one at the front and one at the back,” Brandon, who was covering Trump’s departure from the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey, said in a preview clip from the documentary.

“And I have never seen that before. Forty years doing presidents, never seen that before. I shot it. I shot the shit out of it,” the photojournalist said.

The Washington Post first reported in August how Air Force One acted as a “decoy,” with some White House staff and reporters remaining on board, while the president flew on the other aircraft.

“Beyond showing the lengths the Secret Service will go to protect the president, this installment reveals the cost of that mission: to get him home safely, a plane full of reporters and the public they answer to were left flying blind,” Netflix said.

White House communications director Steven Cheung told NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network, last month, “As the President has said recently, there are many enemies of America who have their sights on him, and we use every tool at our disposal to address those threats.”

articles.title: A new answer to America’s growing elder-care challenges
articles.summary: A common response to America’s growing elder-care needs is one we’ve heard time and again across policy debates: Spend more money the country doesn’t have. But pouring more federal money into a supply-constrained market won’t create the plentiful, affordable options families need.
articles.body:
Last week, the national debt reached $40 trillion for the first time. Worse, our population is aging, and the number of working adults contributing to the tax base is dwindling. This means that the demand for elder care is going to surge, and we cannot afford a government program to paper over the problem.

Elder care is often provided by family members who are juggling jobs, children and other responsibilities, but geography, work and other obligations can make that difficult or impossible. There are few affordable options on the market for elders who don’t have families to take care of them: Non-medical in-home care now costs about $80,000 annually on average for 44 hours of care a week. Nursing home care now exceeds $100,000 annually . Taxpayers often end up shouldering much of those costs, particularly for residential care .

A common response to America’s growing elder-care needs is one we’ve heard time and again across policy debates: Spend more money the country doesn’t have. Scholars at the Brookings Institution, for example, have proposed adding a home-care benefit to Medicare that would extend paid home-care coverage to an estimated 15 million beneficiaries. They estimate that such a benefit would increase taxpayer-funded Medicare spending by roughly $40 billion a year.

But pouring more federal money into a supply-constrained market won’t create the plentiful, affordable options families need.

Instead, policymakers should focus on expanding the supply and range of care available to families. That starts with recognizing a simple fact: Not every older American needs the same kind of help.

Some older Americans need skilled nursing or substantial hands-on assistance, while others need light help preparing meals, getting to appointments, shopping for groceries or keeping up with household tasks. Some may simply need a dependable person around to check in and provide companionship.

Rather than confining families to rigid categories that stymie the supply of care and opportunities to provide it, elder-care policy should foster a continuum of options as varied as families’ needs.

The American Caregivers Act , a federal and state legislative model developed by Independent Women’s Voice, where I work, would take a step in that direction by establishing a framework to allow seniors to host vetted college students who provide limited, non-medical assistance and companionship. Caregivers could help with meals, transportation, errands and light household tasks. In exchange, they would receive room, board and a stipend while continuing their college education.

This plan would offer students an affordable place to live and meaningful caregiving experience while giving seniors and their families a lower-cost option for everyday assistance and companionship. The model draws on the sponsor-based framework used by the State Department’s au pair program , which has long connected families with vetted caregivers, while tailoring rules and protections to senior care.

Families, not taxpayers, would finance the arrangements. The proposal creates no new federal entitlement or taxpayer-funded care benefit.

America can’t avoid the growing care needs of an aging population, but another costly federal entitlement isn’t the answer. Policymakers can make it easier for families to meet those needs by creating room for new, affordable models of care.

Seniors’ needs are diverse. Their options should reflect that.

Heather Madden is the vice president for policy initiatives at Independent Women.
